issues.legal_issue: A person who has perfected title to immovable property by adverse possession may sue to protect that title or recover possession after it is infringed.
material_facts: The Court considered a common legal question in connected matters about whether a person claiming title through adverse possession could sue for declaration, protection of possession, or restoration of possession.
The question included interference or dispossession by a former owner whose title had been extinguished, or by another person.

Earlier decisions had treated adverse possession as available to a plaintiff as well as a defendant; a contrary observation in a later decision had not been contested or supported by consideration of the earlier authorities.
issues.conclusion: A person who has perfected title by adverse possession may use that title as a basis for a suit to protect possession or recover possession, and may sue when any of that person's rights are infringed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 permits a suit for possession based on title, and title includes title perfected by adverse possession. Under Section 27, expiry of the limitation period extinguishes the owner's right; the possessor's perfected right may then be asserted as a plaintiff, not merely raised as a defendant. The Court relied on Sarangadeva Periya Matam v. Ramaswami Goundar, Balkrishan v. Satyaprakash, Des Raj v. Bhagat Ram, Kshitish Chandra Bose v. Commissioner of Ranchi, Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander, Padminibai v. Tangavva, Mohammed Fateh Nasib v. Swarup Chand Hukum Chand, S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina, and Mandal Revenue Officer v. Goundla Venkaiah. It overruled the contrary rule in Gurudwara Sahib v. Gram Panchayat Village Sirthala and decisions relying on it, including State of Uttarakhand v. Mandir Shri Lakshmi Siddh Maharaj and Dharampal v. Punjab Wakf Board.

predicates.kind_civil_property_suit: The proceeding is a civil claim concerning possession or other rights in immovable property.
predicates.claimant_perfected_adverse_title: The claimant acquired title through possession that met the requirements for adverse possession for the legally required period.
predicates.claimant_rights_infringed: Another person interfered with the claimant's rights or dispossessed the claimant.

issues.definition: When a claimant brings a civil property suit after acquiring title through adverse possession and another person infringes the claimant's rights, the claimant may sue on that title.

issues.legal_issue: Title by adverse possession is perfected only through possession that is actual, exclusive, open, continuous, and hostile to the competing owner's title, with the required intention and duration.
material_facts: The Court addressed the requirements governing a claim that possession has matured into title.
The authorities discussed required hostile possession to be sufficiently continuous, public, and extensive, and required the possessor to show an intention to possess against the true owner.
The Court distinguished adverse possession from mere long possession or casual use and stated that the claimant must plead and establish the relevant facts.
issues.conclusion: A claimant must establish the required hostile, open, continuous, and sufficiently extensive possession, together with the necessary intention and duration, to perfect title by adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 governs possession suits based on title, while Section 27 provides for extinguishment of the owner's right at the end of the applicable limitation period. The Court applied the classic requirements nec vi, nec clam, nec precario and relied on P. Lakshmi Reddy v. L. Lakshmi Reddy, S.M. Karim v. Mst. Bibi Sakina, Karnataka Wakf Board v. Government of India, Annakili v. A. Vedanayagam, P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma, T. Anjanappa v. Somalingappa, and Krishnamurthy S. Setlur v. O.V. Narasimha Setty. The claimant must establish actual possession, its commencement and nature, its continuity and publicity, hostility to the owner's title, and the possessor's animus possidendi; mere long possession is insufficient.

rule.if: kind_adverse_title_claim and actual_exclusive_possession and possession_open_and_continuous and possession_hostile_to_owner and possessor_intended_to_exclude_owner and possession_lasted_required_period

predicates.kind_adverse_title_claim: The proceeding involves a claim that possession has matured into title to immovable property.
predicates.actual_exclusive_possession: The claimant actually possessed the property to the exclusion of the competing owner.
predicates.possession_open_and_continuous: The claimant's possession was visible and continued without interruption for the relevant period.
predicates.possession_hostile_to_owner: The claimant possessed the property in denial of the competing owner's title, in a manner sufficiently public to be known or attributable to that owner.
predicates.possessor_intended_to_exclude_owner: The claimant intended to possess the property as an owner and to exclude the competing owner.
predicates.possession_lasted_required_period: The qualifying possession continued for the period required to extinguish the competing owner's right.

issues.definition: A claimant perfects title by adverse possession when the claimant openly, continuously, and exclusively possesses property against the competing owner's title with the required intention for the required period.

issues.legal_issue: A person in possession may seek restoration against a person who dispossesses them otherwise than through due process of law, even before title by adverse possession is perfected.
material_facts: The Court considered the distinction between a possessory claim based on prior possession and a claim based on title perfected by adverse possession.
It stated that a person in possession cannot be ousted by force and that possession may be protected against an unlawful dispossessor before the possessor's title has ripened.
The Court referred to the statutory possessory remedy and the rule that a wrongdoer cannot justify forcible dispossession merely by asserting that title belongs to someone else.
issues.conclusion: A person dispossessed otherwise than through due process may maintain a possessory suit for restoration, including before title by adverse possession is perfected.
issues.legal_principle: Article 64 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides for a suit based on previous possession, and Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides a summary remedy for unlawful dispossession. The Court relied on Lallu Yashwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh, Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander, Somnath Berman v. Dr. S.P. Raju, Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao, and State of U.P. v. Maharaja Dharmander Prasad Singh. These authorities establish that possession is protected against forcible dispossession and that a person must obtain possession through lawful process.

predicates.kind_possessory_claim: The proceeding seeks restoration of possession based on the claimant's prior possession.
predicates.claimant_was_in_possession: The claimant actually possessed the property before the dispossession.
predicates.claimant_was_dispossessed_without_due_pr: Another person removed the claimant from possession without obtaining possession through lawful process.

issues.definition: A claimant who had possession and was dispossessed without lawful process may seek restoration based on prior possession.
